nahhas-irab:1-1.t: The lām was assimilated into the tāʾ and the zāy because of its closeness to them. It is not permissible to pronounce it distinctly (iẓhār) with the lām of definiteness, because of its frequency in speech, but it is permissible with other (lāms) — even though it has been said of this lām that, together with what it is attached to here, it is a proper name. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb said: «al-Tīn» is the mosque of the Companions of the Cave, and al-Zaytūn is «the mosque of Īliyāʾ (Jerusalem)»; so its origin is definiteness, and then naming occurred. Likewise the view of those who said: al-Tīn is Damascus and al-Zaytūn is Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis); and the view of those who said: they are two mosques, one of them being that on which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, spoke to Mūsā ﷺ. As for Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind, he narrated from ʿIkrima and from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: al-Tīn is this fig of yours and al-Zaytūn is your olive. Abū Jaʿfar said: These views, when analysed, come back to one meaning, because the oath is only by the Lord of the worlds, Mighty and Majestic; so the implied form is: "by the Lord of the fig and the olive".

nahhas-irab:2-2.t: It has been said: it is Ṭūr Sīnāʾ, in (various) dialects; and other than this has been said, which we have mentioned.

nahhas-irab:3-3.t:
This is the eloquent dialect. The noun (proper) in it (هذا) is ذا according to the Basrans, and ها is for drawing attention (tanbīh); according to the Kufans, the noun is the dhāl. It is not declined (muʿrab) because it is a noun that is not firmly established (ghayr mutamakkin), shifting (in reference), so it resembles particles; because it is not fixed upon a named thing, it must not be declined. Some grammarians said: because there is an alif at its end, and the alif does not take a vowel. Al-Farrāʾ said: if it were given a vowel it would become a hamza. Al-Khalīl, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the alif is an airy letter, so it is impossible to give it a vowel, because it is in the rank of a vowel, and a vowel is not given a vowel.
Abū Jaʿfar said: «ذا» is an overt noun (ism ẓāhir); what indicates this is the kasra of the lām with it [Translator's note: i.e., لِذا, as with overt nouns, not لَه as with pronouns]. Some grammarians said, in answer to one who asked why pronouns were given vowels but the vague nouns (mubham, demonstratives) were not: pronouns are in the positions of declinable nouns and had a distinction, so they were given vowels. Abū Jaʿfar said: I heard Abū Bakr ibn Shuqayr report this, and it is a good, well-founded answer.
As for al-Farrāʾ, he mixed everything up, saying: whoever says هو زيد with the wāw quiescent says هذا زيد; whoever says هو زيد says هذا أي زيد [Translator's note: the text here is garbled; the vowelling distinguishing the dialectal forms of هو is not shown]; and whoever says هو زيد with doubled wāw says هذاه زيد. Abū Jaʿfar said: The confusion in this is evident, because your saying هو with quiescent wāw is an anomalous dialect, while your saying هذا is a dialect in which the Qur'an came; so how can one be set parallel to the other, unless they correspond from another direction according to his view? That is, in your saying هو, the noun in it according to him is the hāʾ, and the noun in هذا is the dhāl — and this is his view, without disagreement from him. And part of the confusion is that in your saying هذّاه, the hāʾ according to him is for showing the vowel, yet he kept it in connected speech.
Al-Farrāʾ claimed that the evidence that the noun in هذا is the dhāl is the saying of the Arabs in the dual هذان, where they dropped the alif. This is not binding, because the alif only fell in the dual because of the meeting of two quiescent letters; and it was not permissible to convert it, so that one would say هذيان or هذوان, because it is not known to be converted from yāʾ or from wāw so as to be converted back to one of them; so nothing remained but deletion.
الْبَلَدِ الْأَمِينِ is a naʿt (adjective), or if you wish a badal (substitute), or if you wish a ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition). Al-Farrāʾ claimed that الأمين is in the sense of al-āmin (safe), and recited: [al-Ṭawīl] 575-
ألم تعلمي يا أسم ويحك أنّني ... حلفت يمينا لا أخون أميني
(Do you not know, O Asmāʾ — woe to you! — that I swore an oath not to betray the one who trusts me?)
Abū Jaʿfar said: Al-Farrāʾ was opposed in this, and it was said: أمين is in the sense of maʾmūn (made safe / trusted) in both the verse and the line of poetry.

nahhas-irab:4-4.t: The scholars discussed its meaning. From Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: He created everything bent over except man. ʿIkrima said: فِي أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ is youth, strength and endurance. Mujāhid and al-Nakhaʿī said: فِي أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ means in the best form. This is the best of what has been said about it, because the implied form in Arabic is "in a fashioning, the best of fashioning", (أحسن) being put in place of the thing qualified, i.e., in the most balanced fashioning and form.

nahhas-irab:5-5.t:
There is disagreement about it too. From Ibn ʿAbbās: to the most decrepit age; and from ʿIkrima: to the Fire. Muḥammad ibn Jarīr (al-Ṭabarī) claimed that the correct view is "to the most decrepit age", i.e., to senility, and this applies to particular people. He argued for the correctness of this that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, only enumerated what they had witnessed of His power, namely man's passing from youth to senility, and He does not enumerate against them what they do not acknowledge, namely entering the Fire.
Others said: This is not binding, because the proofs of Allah are manifest, and the signs of His Prophet ﷺ have appeared, so everything he informed of must be on the level of what is seen with the eyes.

nahhas-irab:6-6.t:
Whoever said the meaning of "to the lowest of the low" is "to the Fire" made الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا in the position of the accusative as an exception from the hāʾ in رددناه, because it has a plural sense. And whoever said "to the lowest of the low" means "to the most decrepit age" made «الذين» an exception not of the kind of the first (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ). And it has been said: there is an omission in the speech of the thing excepted from.
The implied form is: then We returned him to senility and dotage, until he became unable to worship Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and perform His obligations, and nothing is written for him [Translator's note: the text reads «ولا يكتب له شيء لهم», apparently for "except those who believed …: for them is written the like of what they used to do"] — for them the like of what they used to do. Ibn Abī Ṭalḥa narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: فَلَهُمْ أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, he said: He says: undiminished.

nahhas-irab:7-7.t:
The grammarians discussed this word (بعد), its explanation, the difference in its vowel, its nunation and lack of nunation, with more than ten answers. Among that is that the grammarians agree that قبل and بعد, when they are "terminal" (ghāyatān, i.e., cut off from their muḍāf ilayhi), are in origin not to be declined. They gave several answers as to the reason for that. Among the soundest is that the way nouns are made definite is by alif-lām or by annexation to a definite noun; so since these two were made definite by other than the definiteness of nouns, their being indeclinable (mabnī) became necessary. ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān said: because they are dependent on what comes after them. And it has been said: since they do not move through the various case forms and are not firmly established (lam yatamakkanā), indeclinability became necessary for them. These are three answers.
If it is said: why was a vowel necessary for them? The answer is that Sībawayh said: "As for the firmly established noun that is put in a position in the rank of the non-established, it is their saying: ابدأ بهذا أوّل, and يا حكم أقبل". The explanation of this is that since أول, قبل and بعد had to be undeclined in one position while being declined in others, it was disliked to leave them without a vowel, so they were given ḍamma.
If it is said: why were they not given fatḥa or kasra? There are five answers to this question. Among them: adverbs (ẓurūf) take the accusative and genitive when they are not affected, and do not take the nominative; so when they were affected they took ḍamma, because ḍamma is of the kind of the nominative, which does not enter them in their sound state. And it has been said: since they resembled the singular vocative, they were given its vowel. And it has been said: since they are a terminus (ghāya), they were given the ultimate (ghāya) of vowels. These are three answers concerning the ḍamma, from the Basrans; we know of no others from them. The other two answers are from the Kufans. Al-Farrāʾ said: since قبل and بعد comprise two meanings, they were given ḍamma. Abū Jaʿfar said: The explanation of this is that they comprise their own meaning and the meaning of what comes after them, so they were given the heaviest of vowels. And Hishām said: it was not permissible to give them fatḥa, for then they would be as though annexed to what comes after them; nor kasra, for then they would be like what is annexed to the speaker [Translator's note: the text reads «المخاطب», "the addressee"]; so nothing remained but ḍamma. Abū Jaʿfar said: These are nine answers.
Al-Farrāʾ permitted آتيك بعدٌ يا هذا ("I will come to you afterwards, O you") with ḍamma and nunation, and recited: [al-Ṭawīl] 576-
ونحن قتلنا الأزد أزد شنوءة ... فما شربوا بعد على لذّة خمرا
(We killed al-Azd, Azd Shanūʾa, and afterwards they never drank wine with pleasure.)
Abū Jaʿfar said: This is outside what the Qur'an, the speech of the Arabs and reason have brought. He has no proof in the line, if its author is even known, because without nunation it is permissible (metrically) according to the experts in prosody, just as they recited: [al-Ṭawīl] 577-
شاقتك أحداج سليمى بعاقل ... فعيناك للبين تجودان بالدّمع
(Sulaymā's camel-litters at ʿĀqil have stirred your longing, so your eyes pour tears at the parting.)
He also permitted رأيتك بعدًا يا هذا. Abū Jaʿfar said: This is a parallel; that is, he may have intended the indefinite. And Hishām permitted رأيتك بعدَ يا هذا, making it accusative and implying the muḍāf ilayhi, as though he claimed it had been pronounced since it was intended. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Akhfash claimed that the meaning is: "so who will deny you, after (this), concerning the Judgement?" Abū Jaʿfar said: This is not to be relied upon; «ما» does not occur in the sense of «من» except anomalously. The meaning here is sound, i.e., "so what drives you, O denier — what thing drives you to denial, after the appearance of the proofs and evidences, of the Judgement, whose news was brought by the one with the most manifest proofs?"

nahhas-irab:8-8.t: I.e., in His management and His making, no corruption or inconsistency enters your religion — and others are not like that.
